title: Can directed reachability have near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth?
formal: Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Both bounds must hold on arbitrary inputs, including sparse graphs with long directed paths. Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.
context:
A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.

The size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.

Shortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.

The August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”
why: I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.
definitions:
The model is a standard word-based PRAM/shared-memory parallel model, with $O(\log n)$-bit words and concurrent access handled by standard PRAM conventions. Local primitive operations, auxiliary data construction, and shortcut generation count toward work. $\widetilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors. High probability means $1-n^{-c}$ for a requested fixed $c>0$. The output is reachability, not shortest-path distances.

For definiteness fix a CREW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed, and concurrent writes to one cell are prohibited. Word operations are arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of logarithmic-size words. The target permits the polylogarithmic overhead of simulating common alternative PRAM conventions.

progress.text: Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford obtain almost-linear work with $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ depth for directed reachability.

Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak improve the near-linear-work depth bound as graph density increases; their dense-graph reachability bound is $n^{0.136}$. The theorem does not give polylogarithmic depth for every density.

Kogan and Parter give polylogarithmic depth with $\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})$ work, where $T=|TC(G)|$ and $\omega$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent. Even the hypothetical $\omega=2$ gives work in terms of $T$, which may be quadratic for a linear-size input.

status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 closure-sensitive algorithm. Near-linear input work with polylogarithmic depth remains the target.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm meeting the work, depth, and error guarantees simultaneously on all directed inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the specified PRAM model. Work measured by transitive-closure size is insufficient.

importance.reason: Combining near-linear work with polylogarithmic depth for directed reachability would resolve a major barrier in efficient parallel graph algorithms.
